title: How to Create a Retirement Plan for a Family-Owned Business
description: Succession planning, liquidity events, and diversification for owners.
content:
For family business owners, the business *is* the retirement plan. This is a high-risk strategy. If the industry shifts, the economy crashes, or the next generation fails to lead, your nest egg evaporates. A robust retirement plan for business owners requires separating personal wealth from business equity. You must build a 'Side Fund' of liquid assets (stocks/bonds) and create a formal exit strategy—whether that means selling to a competitor, selling to employees (ESOP), or passing it to children.

Key Takeaways

  • Diversification is Survival: Do not reinvest 100% of profits. Siphon 20% of net income annually into a diversified portfolio (401k/Brokerage). If the business goes to zero, you must still be able to retire.
  • Defined Benefit Plans: High-income owners can set up Cash Balance Plans to contribute $100k-$300k/year tax-deductible. This is the fastest way to move cash from the business to your personal name.
  • The 'Key Person' Risk: If the business cannot run without you, it has no sellable value. You own a job, not an asset. You must build systems and a team to make the entity transferrable.
  • Buy-Sell Agreements: If you have partners, you need a funded Buy-Sell agreement (often backed by life insurance) to ensure your spouse gets cashed out if you die.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The sale of a business often triggers a massive Capital Gains tax bill. Strategies like 'Installment Sales' or 'Charitable Remainder Trusts' can spread this tax hit over years or eliminate it entirely.

Exit Options

How to monetize your life's work.

Option 1: Sale to Third Party

Pros: Maximum cash upfront. Clean break.
Cons: Taxes (20% Fed + State). Loss of legacy.
Metric: Businesses typically sell for 3x-6x EBITDA. Is that enough to retire on?

Option 2: Internal Succession (Kids/Managers)

Structure: You sell the business to them via a promissory note. They pay you monthly from future profits.
Pros: Acts like a pension. Keeps legacy alive.
Cons: You carry the risk. If they run it into the ground, the payments stop.

Option 3: ESOP (Employee Stock Ownership Plan)

Structure: Sell to employees.
Pros: Massive tax benefits (can defer capital gains). Good for culture.
Cons: High setup costs ($50k+). Only works for larger small businesses ($2M+ revenue).

The 'Outside' Pot

  1. The Landlord Play: Own the building personally (in an LLC). Rent it to the business. When you sell the business, keep the building. The rent provides retirement income.
  2. Solo 401(k) / SEP IRA: Max these every single year. Treat it as a mandatory payroll expense, not discretionary profit sharing.
  3. Valuation Check: Every 3-5 years, get a professional valuation. Don't guess what your business is worth. Base your retirement math on real numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I gift the business to my kids?

Yes, but it uses up your Lifetime Gift Tax Exemption ($13.6M in 2025). If the value is higher, you pay 40% tax. 'Freezing' the value via an IDGT (Trust) is a common workaround.

What if I don't want to retire?

Keep owning it, but hire a GM (General Manager). Transition from CEO to Chairman. Take distributions, not salary.

Should I count the business in my Net Worth?

For ego? Yes. For retirement planning? No. Count it as $0 until the check clears. It is an illiquid, high-risk asset.
